title: Lens accuracy versus word length
takeaway: Across multi-hop prompts whose unspoken intermediate concept is one to four-plus tokens long, the J-lens decodes and swaps single-token concepts well and then falls off sharply as the concept grows longer, while the template lens holds roughly flat at every length. On single-token concepts the two are comparable, with the template lens slightly behind on readout and ahead on swaps.
walkthrough:
The figure is a live two-panel line chart, and it carries the quantitative case for the [[template-lens]]. The [[jacobian-lens]] derives one vector per vocabulary token, so a concept whose name spans several tokens has no vector of its own — the [[single-token-limitation]]. The template lens was built to cover such concepts, and this figure reports how each lens holds up as the latent word grows longer.

Both panels share an x axis of word length in tokens, bucketed as 1, 2, 3 and 4+, with the number of items in each bucket printed underneath. Both y axes run from 0% to 100%. Three series are drawn, each a line through the four buckets with a vertical [[wilson-interval|95% Wilson interval]] at every point.

The left panel, "Decoding the intermediate concept", measures readout. The prompts are multi-hop questions whose bridging concept is never written out, similar in kind to the [[multihop-benchmark]] but chosen so that the concept's length varies. A trial counts as a success when that concept appears in the lens's top ten at the read position.

The right panel, "Swapping the intermediate concept", measures a causal test instead. A [[lens-coordinate-swap]] exchanges one concept's lens coordinate for another's across the whole [[workspace-layers|workspace layer range]], at [[swap-strength-alpha|swap strength]] $\alpha = 1$. The trial succeeds when the model's answer follows the concept that was swapped in.

The shapes of the lines are the result. The J-lens first-token series starts near the ceiling on one-token words and then drops: 98%, 48%, 32% and 7% on readout, and 45%, 5%, 8% and 0% on swaps. Averaging the lens scores over the word's constituent tokens does not repair this, and that dashed series sits at or below the solid one in every bucket.

The template lens stays roughly level across all four buckets, at 94% to 100% on readout and 62% down to 43% on swaps. On single-token words it trails the J-lens slightly on readout and leads it on swaps.

The per-bucket counts are small, between 14 and 54 items, so the intervals are wide. Hovering a point prints its raw count, such as 14/29. The evidence supports the direction of the trend rather than any single point.

terms.definition: The first legend series, drawn as a solid line with filled markers. For a multi-token concept it uses the J-lens vector of only the concept's first token, so "photosynthesis" is scored through the fragment phot.

The second legend series, drawn as a dashed line with open markers. It averages the J-lens scores over all the tokens the concept word breaks into, as a fairer attempt at reading a multi-token concept out of a single-token lens.

The third legend series, drawn as a solid line in orange. The template lens builds one vector per word by averaging residual-stream activations over passages that end just before that word, then centering and whitening those means.

The step that multiplies the centered per-word mean by the inverse of the residual stream's covariance matrix (with a small ridge term). It converts a raw class mean into a linear discriminant direction, and it is what the legend word "whitened" refers to.

One direction in residual-stream space per vocabulary token per layer, obtained from the Jacobian of the model's output with respect to activations. It is the unit both lenses' readouts and swaps operate on, and its one-per-token construction is what limits it to single-token names.
The readout panel. It asks whether the latent concept can be named from the activation, with no intervention on the model.
The intervention panel. It asks whether writing a different concept into the same lens coordinates changes what the model answers.
The readout success measure: the share of prompts on which the true latent concept lands somewhere in the lens's ten highest-scoring entries at the read position.

terms.term: "P(answer follows the swap) at α = 1" (right y-axis label)
terms.definition: The swap success measure: the share of pairs on which the model's output changes to the answer implied by the concept swapped in. α = 1 names the swap magnitude used.

The multiplier on a lens-coordinate swap. At α = 1 the source concept's projection is removed and a matched-magnitude target projection is added; the paper elsewhere reports that α = 2 raises success rates, so α = 1 is the conservative setting.

terms.term: "tokens in the latent word" (left x-axis label)
terms.definition: The bucketing variable in the readout panel: how many tokens the model's tokenizer splits the unspoken intermediate concept into.

terms.term: "tokens in the anchor word" (right x-axis label)
terms.definition: The bucketing variable in the swap panel: the token length of the concept word that defines the swap pair. It is the same length variable as on the left, applied to the pair rather than to a single readout.

The bridging entity a multi-hop question requires but never states, such as Mars in a question about the fourth planet's color. It is the thing the lens is asked to name and the thing the swap replaces.

Two-hop factual questions whose surface tokens have no direct association with the answer, so the model must compute a bridging entity first. The prompts here are of that kind but were selected so the bridging entity's token length varies from one to four.
One item in the right panel: a source concept present in the activation and a target concept written in its place, together with the answer the target concept implies.

The band of middle layers, roughly L38 to L92 on the paper's percent-of-depth scale, in which the J-space behaves like a workspace. Every swap in this figure is applied across the whole band rather than at one layer.
The four x-axis positions. The last bucket pools every concept of four or more tokens, since individual longer lengths would have too few items.

The small gray counts printed under each bucket tick, giving how many items that bucket holds. They differ between the two panels because the swap evaluation uses fewer items than the readout evaluation.

The vertical line at each point, spanning the 95% Wilson interval for that proportion. The Wilson form is used because it stays sensible at rates of 0% and 100% and at small counts, both of which occur here.
The cutoff that defines readout success. The lens ranks a large vocabulary at the read position, and only the ten highest-scoring entries count as a hit.
The visual coding of the token-average J-lens series, distinguishing it from the first-token J-lens series drawn in the same color with filled markers.
Text shown on a point, giving the series label, the bucket, the raw successes over trials, and the percentage — for example "whitened template lens / 2 tok: 28/29 (97%)".
The three series are nudged a few pixels apart at each bucket so their markers and error bars do not overlap. The offset carries no meaning.

numbers.meaning: The total number of multi-hop prompts in the readout panel, the sum of its four buckets. The caption reports this figure.
The readout panel's item counts for buckets 1, 2, 3 and 4+. Single-token intermediates are the largest group because common concepts more often have single-token names.
The total number of swap pairs in the right panel, split as 53 single-token and 59 multi-token. It is smaller than 126 because not every readout prompt yields a usable source-target pair.
The swap panel's item counts for buckets 1, 2, 3 and 4+, summing to 112. The multi-token buckets sum to 59.

Readout success for the J-lens read at the concept's first token, across the four length buckets. Near-perfect at one token, then falling by roughly half at each further token, which is the degradation the appendix reports.
Readout success for the J-lens averaged over the concept's constituent tokens. It is below the first-token variant in every bucket, which is why the appendix says that averaging does not help.

Readout success for the template lens. It is flat within the noise across all four lengths, and slightly below the J-lens at one token — the paper's "slightly underperforming on readouts" for single-token concepts.
Swap success for the first-token J-lens. Swapping a first-token fragment such as tch for beeth almost never redirects the answer once the concept is longer than one token.
Swap success for the token-averaged J-lens. It matches the first-token variant at one and two tokens and is marginally worse at three, so averaging again buys nothing.

Swap success for the template lens. It is roughly level across lengths and clearly above the J-lens at one token — the paper's "modestly overperforming the J-lens on swaps." The 4+ bucket is lower, but with 14 items its interval reaches from 21% to 67%.
The confidence level of the Wilson intervals drawn as error bars on every point.
The two 0/15 and 0/14 points still carry an interval reaching about 20% and 22%. Zero successes out of fifteen trials does not establish that the true rate is zero.
The swap strength used for every point in the right panel: remove the source projection, add a target projection of matched magnitude, once over.
The rank cutoff for a readout hit. It is a lenient threshold relative to a top-1 criterion, chosen because the ranking universe is large.
The four token-length buckets on the x axis. Four-plus is pooled because longer concepts are rare in the prompt set.
The y-axis ticks in both panels. Both axes are identical, so the two panels' heights can be compared directly even though they measure different things.
The number of series plotted: two J-lens variants and the template lens. The two J-lens variants share a color and are separated by line dash and marker fill.

The size of the template lens's predefined word vocabulary, built elsewhere in the appendix. It is the ranking universe behind the template lens's readouts, and the reason the method needs its vocabulary enumerated in advance.
The workspace layer band, on the paper's 0–100 percent-of-depth scale, over which every swap in the right panel is applied.
